bull_thesis: Centrus is the only U.S.-owned, U.S.-technology uranium enricher, and it holds the only U.S. license to enrich to the 19.75% HALEU (high-assay low-enriched uranium) grade that next-generation reactors need. That is a genuine regulatory-license moat: nearly 4 million proven machine-hours, a running demonstration cascade at Piketon, Ohio, and a first-mover position competitors would need years and tens of millions of dollars to replicate. The macro backdrop is real and durable: Russia's exit from the Western enrichment market removes roughly 6.5 million SWU (separative work units, the unit of enrichment) of supply, U.S. reactor restarts and uprates add demand, and the enrichment price curve has compounded about 24% a year from 2019 to 2025. Government validation arrived on schedule -- the Department of Energy signed a $900 million HALEU award (potential total ~$1.07B with options) and the NNSA signaled intent to sole-source certain national-security enrichment. The balance sheet is a fortress: roughly $2B cash, net cash of about $690M (~$31 per share), enough to fund the early build and wait. If Centrus executes its base-case build-out -- 12 metric tons of HALEU, first new cascade online in 2029 -- and pricing holds, today's ~$449M-revenue trading business becomes a multi-billion-dollar enrichment franchise with a national-security premium. The $2.3B contingent backlog is the option on that future. Returns are already respectable (return on capital ~15%, return on equity ~25%), so this is not a broken business -- it is an infrastructure story with a government sponsor.
bear_thesis: The stock prices a plant that does not yet exist. On today's numbers Centrus trades at roughly 100x free cash flow with trailing-twelve-month free cash flow actually NEGATIVE (about -$61M), revenue essentially flat (+1.5% year over year to $449M), and earnings per share falling ~13% because the share count is climbing. Every intrinsic-value method -- discounted cash flow (~$64 fair value), earnings power, Graham, owner-earnings -- reads a deeply negative margin of safety versus the ~$175 price (roughly -83% to -100%). The load-bearing catalyst has already fired: the DOE award the entire 2025 narrative waited for was announced in January 2026 and its contract signed July 1, 2026. What remains is not an asymmetric event; it is a five-year, capital-intensive construction project -- 2026 guidance is for revenue roughly flat and capital spend of $350-500M, i.e. a build that consumes cash and delivers first HALEU only in 2029 and its contracted metric ton by 2032. The build is being funded by serial shareholder dilution: two at-the-market share-sale programs plus convertibles, share count up ~15% in a year, and management's own tell -- launching a $1 billion program precisely because the stock was high. Insiders sold ~129,000 shares open-market with zero purchases. Competition is the quiet risk: the DOE is deliberately funding a SECOND domestic enricher, so the license moat erodes over the very horizon this build occupies. Piotroski score 3/9 and a Q3 2025 gross loss underline how thin and mix-dependent current economics are. The 'deep value' screen tag is a false read caused by a lumpy trailing multiple; on intrinsic methods this is one of the most expensive names in the universe.
consensus_delta: For a deep-value name the right question is whether the street is pricing terminal decline into a stable earner. Here it is the opposite: the street is pricing a terminal BOOM into a business with flat revenue and negative free cash flow. The sell-side consensus target of ~$224 (+38%) and the narrative of a 'nuclear renaissance' assume flawless execution of an unbuilt 2029 plant, sustained record SWU pricing, and eventual government price support -- while the company itself gives no financial guidance beyond spending and its CFO's first act was to launch a $1 billion share-sale program. Where we disagree with the market: the market treats the $900M DOE award and the HALEU license as a mispriced, still-ahead catalyst; in fact the award is already signed (July 1, 2026) and the license is known -- both are IN the price. Analyst-target velocity is already rolling over (-26% versus the year-ago average target), and smart-money and institutional-flow scores are weak (5/100 and 50/100). The genuinely contrarian call is that this richly-valued momentum story, near its 52-week lows and still ~100x free cash flow, is a value TRAP dressed as a value name -- optically cheap on a trailing multiple, extraordinarily expensive on intrinsic worth.
forcing_function: The event that would have forced a re-rating -- the DOE HALEU award -- has already happened and is signed (announced January 5, 2026; contract signed July 1, 2026). The re-rate is spent. The remaining dated events are execution milestones that consume cash rather than release value: the first 'Certified for Construction' work package and construction-partner mobilization in 2026, first new cascade online in 2029, and the contracted one metric ton of HALEU due by March 2032. For a value convergence you would need a NEW forcing function -- a firm government price-floor (the MP Materials precedent management admits it has no visibility into), a binding strategic investment from KHNP/POSCO or a hyperscaler converting the MOU to cash, or a de-contingency of the $2.3B backlog. None is dated or committed. Absent that, the next 'forcing function' is the market's own recognition, quarter by quarter, that a spent catalyst and negative free cash flow do not support ~100x.
valley_of_death: The next 3-9 months carry the classic build-phase squeeze. 2026 guidance is for revenue roughly flat ($425-475M) against capital spend of $350-500M -- the company will spend far more than it earns, so reported free cash flow stays negative (already -$61M trailing). Quarterly results will remain violently lumpy on delivery mix (Q3 2025 posted an outright gross loss), which can shock a momentum shareholder base. Most important, the funding mechanism itself is the near-term risk: the active $1 billion at-the-market program means Centrus is issuing new shares into any strength, a continuous, mechanical dilution headwind, and the CFO has signaled more partnership/capital work to come. There is no debt-maturity wall (net cash ~$690M) and no solvency crisis (Altman-Z 2.3) -- the danger is not bankruptcy, it is that flat earnings plus visible dilution plus a spent catalyst removes the fuel that carried a 100x multiple, and the stock de-rates toward intrinsic value long before the 2029 first-cascade payoff.
positioning_washout: This is not a yield/dividend name, so there is no coupon-driven forced exit. The mechanical pressure runs the other way: it is a momentum/thematic-nuclear holder base (retail and thematic-ETF flows into the uranium/enrichment trade) sitting on a stock near its 52-week lows after a ~34% drop below its 200-day average. The washout risk is a de-rating unwind -- once the signed DOE award removes the 'awaiting catalyst' story and each quarter prints negative free cash flow plus fresh share issuance, thematic momentum money can leave as quickly as it arrived, and the ongoing at-the-market program adds a steady supply of new shares on top. There is no natural stabilizing buyer (insiders are net sellers, smart-money score 5/100). The clean, mechanically-forced-seller setup the regime favors is absent here; what exists instead is a slow bleed as a saturated narrative deflates.
moderator_conclusion: Pass for now. Centrus is a real company with a genuine narrow moat -- the only U.S. HALEU enrichment license, proven technology, a fortress net-cash balance sheet (~$690M), and a growing, government-backed demand story as Russia exits the Western market. Management is credible on milestones and delivered the biggest one: the $900 million DOE award. But this is the wrong instrument at the wrong price. The 'deep value' tag is a false read from a lumpy trailing multiple; on every intrinsic method the stock trades at a deeply negative margin of safety, roughly 2.3x our reconciled base-case sum-of-parts of ~$75 against a ~$175 quote -- and even the favorable sum-of-parts (~$113) sits below today's price. Reading the current regime confirms the pass: the market is in a dispersion phase that rewards hard-dated, mechanically-forced special situations in thin-coverage lanes, and PENALIZES spent catalysts and single-factor thematic bets. Centrus fails both tests -- its load-bearing catalyst already fired, and its thesis hinges on one shared macro driver (the nuclear-capacity/SWU-price wave) with no resolution-driver independence. What is left is a five-year construction project financed by continuous shareholder dilution (share count +15% in a year, an active $1B at-the-market program, insiders net sellers), with first production in 2029. The payoff, if it comes, is a 2029-2032 story, not a 2026 one, and you are being asked to pre-pay for flawless execution. The reward is negative across every reconciled scenario. On value grounds alone -- ignoring the spent catalyst entirely -- this is the lowest tier: an optically-cheap trailing multiple masking one of the richest intrinsic valuations in the book. Pass.
sop_breakdown: Reconciled base case ~$75/share, versus a ~$175 market price. Core operating enrichment/trading business ~$45 (blend of the DCF ~$64 favorable anchor and the ~$26 intrinsic-method cluster, weighted toward the conservative side given negative trailing free cash flow, flat revenue, and a Q3 gross loss). Plus net cash ~$690M = ~$31/share, haircut modestly to ~$25 for the announced $350-500M annual capex that will consume it and the ongoing at-the-market dilution. Plus a small ~$5/share risk-adjusted credit for the now-signed $900M DOE award and $2.3B contingent backlog optionality. No listed enrichment peer exists to cross-check a multiple, so the anchor is intrinsic value not relative -- and every intrinsic method reads far below the tape. Fair value ~$75 implies the market is paying roughly 2.3x our base-case intrinsic value for execution on an unbuilt plant.
risk_reward: Deeply unfavorable. Downside to a base-case fair value of ~$75 is about -57% from ~$175; downside to the adverse parts (~$46) is about -74%. Upside to the favorable parts (~$113) is still about -35% BELOW today's price -- i.e. even the bull sum-of-parts does not reach the current quote. There is essentially no margin of safety; the reward is negative across every reconciled scenario, with the only path to justifying the price being flawless multi-year execution plus sustained record enrichment pricing plus government price support that management admits it has no visibility into.
peer_comps_note: There is no listed enrichment peer -- Urenco, Orano, Rosatom and TENEX are all state-owned or unlisted, and the nearest public proxy (Cameco, CCJ) is a miner, not an enricher. The peer read is therefore an intrinsic one, not a relative one, and the peer file's verdict is 'rich vs peers': price-to-free-cash-flow ~103x with a deeply negative margin of safety across every valuation method, a valuation resting on long-duration HALEU/national-security optionality rather than current cash flows. This is NOT a discount-to-peers value setup; if anything the scarcity of comps has let the multiple run far ahead of any cash-flow anchor. The screener's 'deep value' tag is an artifact of a lumpy trailing multiple, not a genuine cheapness signal.

bull_thesis:
The bullish case is that Centrus Energy is the only company in the United States licensed and physically able to enrich uranium with American technology, that Washington has now put more than a billion dollars behind it in a signed contract, and that the shares have already fallen about 62% from their 52-week high of $464.25 to $175.78 (New York close, 28 August 2026) while the underlying position got stronger rather than weaker.

Start with what is genuinely proven. The company has run its Piketon, Ohio cascade continuously for more than two years, has logged over 3.9 million machine hours across its centrifuge programme, and has delivered more than 1.6 metric tons of high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU - fuel enriched to just under 20%, which next-generation reactors need and which no other American plant can legally make) to the Department of Energy. Crucially, it delivered ahead of schedule: the July 2026 announcement confirms an additional 900 kilograms completed early. The customer with the deepest possible visibility into this operation responded by extending the contract, then signing a definitive one worth over $1 billion including options on 1 July 2026. That is the single hardest piece of third-party validation available.

The regulatory barrier is real and management can describe it precisely. As the chief executive put it in the first-quarter 2025 call, Centrus holds the only licence permitting enrichment up to 19.75%, and building a competing plant from scratch "takes years and tens of millions of dollars" just to get permitted. Urenco's American affiliate is not licensed for this material; Orano and the laser-enrichment venture are at the announcement stage. For the rest of the decade the competitive set in domestic high-assay fuel is one company.

Demand is not speculative either. Russia's exit from the Western market removes roughly 6.5 million separative work units (the industry's unit of enrichment) of near-term American demand that has to be sourced somewhere else, and management notes the enrichment price curve compounded at about 24% a year from 2019 to 2025. Commercial commitments are converting from talk into contracts: the August 2026 agreement with X-energy is a definitive supply contract that potentially includes customer prepayments, a genuine step up from the 2025 memorandum with the Korean utility KHNP and POSCO. Contracted backlog has grown from $2.3 billion at the end of 2025 to about $4.5 billion, with the contingent enrichment slice alone reaching $3.0 billion.

Execution risk is being deliberately bought down. Fluor - one of the world's larger engineering and construction firms - is the primary contractor at Piketon. Geiger Brothers, who built the existing cascade, handles the ground work. Palantir's data platform is being used to run the supply chain, and management has claimed roughly $300 million of identified cost reductions since January 2026. Hiring is running ahead of plan in both Ohio and Tennessee, and 2026 revenue guidance was raised in May to $450-500 million from $425-475 million.

The balance sheet buys the time this needs. At 30 June 2026 the company held $1.87 billion of cash against $1.18 billion of convertible debt - net cash of $691 million, or about $31.60 for each of the 21.9 million fully diluted shares. Management also has a $1 billion at-the-market equity facility available and a government contract that is a procurement, not a loan, so it neither dilutes nor levers.

What has to hold for this to work: the first new cascade must come online in 2029 as promised; the total construction bill must land near the roughly $2.8 billion implied by the European benchmark management itself volunteered ($2 billion for 2.5 million separative work units), not far above it; enrichment prices must stay near current levels rather than collapsing when Urenco and Orano add capacity in the 2030s; and the brokerage business must be bridged across 2028, when the waivers permitting Russian-sourced imports expire and before the new plant produces. If all four hold, a business running 3.5 million separative work units a year at mature cost is worth several billion dollars, and today's price will look like an entry point.
bear_thesis:
The bearish case does not require the plant to fail. It only requires the plant to be worth roughly what it costs - and for investors to notice that they are paying $3.8 billion today for a business that currently earns almost nothing.

Start with the earnings. Over the last twelve months Centrus produced $473.9 million of revenue and $7.4 million of operating profit - a margin of 1.6%. Reported net income of $48.5 million looks far better, but the gap is interest earned on the cash pile, and that cash was raised from investors rather than generated by the business. In the March 2026 quarter operating income was $0.8 million; in the June quarter it was $10.4 million. Strip out the interest and there is no profitable operating company here at all. Free cash flow over the same twelve months was negative $222 million, and it is deteriorating on purpose: capital spending went from $4.4 million in the September 2025 quarter to $94.8 million in the June 2026 quarter, with full-year guidance of $350-500 million and several billion still to come.

The cash that supposedly protects the downside was bought, not earned. Across the last four quarters the company raised roughly $1.22 billion externally - $782 million of convertible notes in the September 2025 quarter, $384 million of stock in December, and $54 million of at-the-market sales in June 2026 - while burning $222 million. Shares outstanding rose from 16.98 million to 19.88 million in five quarters, dilution of about 17%, and the $1 billion equity facility remains open. A falling share price makes each future dollar raised more dilutive, which is the classic reflexive trap for a company that must issue equity to finish a build.

Then there is the part almost nobody discusses: roughly three-quarters of current revenue comes from buying enriched uranium abroad - historically from Russia's TENEX - and reselling it to American utilities. That business has no moat, erratic margins, and a legislated end date. Management disclosed in the third-quarter 2025 call that waivers cover committed deliveries in 2026 and 2027 only. The first new cascade is scheduled for 2029. Across five consecutive earnings calls, not one analyst asked how the company bridges 2028, and management never volunteered it. The most likely shape of the next two years is therefore a shrinking revenue base, an accelerating cash burn, and continued equity issuance.

The economics of the build are undisclosed and unverifiable. Analysts have asked directly and repeatedly for the price per separative work unit Centrus realises and its cost to produce one. The chief executive refused in the third-quarter 2025 call: naming it "will point to our cost structure." The chief financial officer, asked in the second-quarter 2025 call how far the cash would stretch, did not answer, and instead volunteered a European competitor's cost of about $2 billion for 2.5 million separative work units - which implies roughly $2.8 billion for Centrus's planned 3.5 million, against $1.87 billion of cash. That is the only cost anchor on the record, it came from management, and it points to a funding gap. The claimed "$300 million in potential cost savings" cannot be checked because no project budget has ever been published; a saving measured against an undisclosed number is unfalsifiable.

The presentation is drifting promotional. In the June 2026 quarter reported net income of $16.8 million was accompanied by an adjusted figure of $38.7 million - a $22 million gap, the widest yet - while stock-based compensation of $18.1 million in that single quarter exceeded reported profit. Gross margin fell to 28.3% from 34.9% a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share fell 52% year on year. Headline backlog of $4.5 billion is not comparable to an ordinary industrial backlog: management itself labels the $3.0 billion enrichment slice "contingent," meaning contingent on capacity that does not exist, and only about $700 million is deliverable from today's business.

Insiders are voting the other way. Over the most bullish stretch in the company's history there were zero open-market purchases against eight sales totalling 128,839 shares. And the takeover-and-activist route that normally disciplines a company spending shareholders' money for five years before returning any is blocked: the Section 382 rights agreement, a poison-pill mechanism, was extended for a seventh time on 18 June 2026.

Finally, this is not an independent bet. On 28 August 2026 the shares fell 9.8% in one session while Cameco fell 5.9%, Uranium Energy 9.0%, Denison 7.6%, Energy Fuels 6.8%, Oklo 5.6%, NuScale 4.6% and the uranium exchange-traded fund 5.8%. Nothing company-specific happened. The entire position is a levered claim on one shared driver - the market's appetite for the nuclear and artificial-intelligence power build-out - and with no current earnings to cushion it, that claim reprices violently. The 52-week range of $142.13 to $464.25 is the honest picture of how this security behaves.

What would confirm the bear case: a September-quarter result in early November showing another weak delivery quarter against a now much larger cost base; any use of the equity facility at a depressed price; a 2027 guidance package in February that fails to bridge the post-waiver revenue gap; or the first published total project cost coming in above $3 billion.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about whether the plant gets built - we think it probably does - but about what a 2029 asset with undisclosed economics is worth in 2026.

Three street assumptions look wrong. First, the market is treating headline backlog of about $4.5 billion as though it were an ordinary industrial order book. It is not, and management says so in its own words: the roughly $3.0 billion enrichment slice is described as "contingent," contingent on capacity that does not exist. Only about $700 million is brokerage backlog deliverable from today's business. Backlog that requires $3 billion of construction before it converts is a capital-expenditure plan wearing a revenue label.

Second, the market is capitalising the wrong earnings number. Trailing net income of $48.5 million is widely quoted; trailing operating income is $7.4 million. The difference is interest earned on $1.87 billion of cash that shareholders and convertible bondholders supplied. On the operating business - a 1.6% margin - there is nothing yet to capitalise. The June 2026 quarter made this unusually visible: reported profit of $16.8 million against an adjusted figure of $38.7 million, with stock-based compensation of $18.1 million in the quarter alone exceeding the reported number.

Third, and most striking, the street is carrying a revenue base that legislation is scheduled to remove. The waivers permitting the imports that feed the brokerage business cover committed deliveries in 2026 and 2027 only, as management disclosed in the November 2025 call. The first new cascade is due in 2029. Across five consecutive earnings calls, no analyst asked how 2028 is bridged. That is a full year in which the old business is gone and the new one has not started, sitting inside every published forecast without being modelled.

Worth noting that the consensus figure itself is stale rather than live. The quoted target of $225 is an average across eighteen targets over the past year that averaged $234.50; over the last month only four targets have been published and they average $199, with UBS at $185 on 19 August and Roth Capital at $171 on 27 July. The analyst community is already marking down toward our view - the headline consensus simply has not caught up. Where we go further than they do is on the funding path: a company that must issue equity into a falling share price to finish a build is in a reflexive loop the current targets do not contemplate.
forcing_function:
There is no binding event inside our eighteen-month view that forces a re-rating in either direction, and that is itself the finding.

The events that were supposed to force one have fired. The Department of Energy contract was signed on 1 July 2026 at over $1 billion including options. Index inclusion took effect on 14 July 2026. The X-energy definitive supply agreement was signed on 6 August 2026. In the six weeks since the last of those, the shares have gone nowhere and then fallen 9.8% on a sector day - which tells you the market has already absorbed all three.

What remains is a list of soft items. Management has guided to completing the first commercially manufactured centrifuge at Oak Ridge by the end of 2026 - a genuine engineering proof point, and the one item that could plausibly move sentiment positively, but it is guidance rather than a commitment and it produces no revenue. The National Nuclear Security Administration signalled an intent to sole-source certain enrichment work and the company confirmed in May 2026 that it had responded, but there is no date, no announced value, and management explicitly declines to predict it. The Oklo deconversion joint venture is still described as being explored.

The two dated items that will actually matter are both potential negatives. The September-quarter result in early November 2026 lands the first large capital-spending numbers into the accounts against the company's historically weakest delivery quarter. The February 2027 annual guidance forces management to say, publicly and for the first time, what 2028 revenue looks like after the import waivers expire and before the new cascades run.

The disclosure that would genuinely force a re-rating - a published total project cost and a realised price per separative work unit - is entirely within management's control and has been declined on five consecutive calls. Until those two numbers exist, no outside investor can compute the return on this project, and the share price will keep being set by sentiment toward the nuclear theme rather than by analysis of the asset.
valley_of_death:
The risky window runs from now through roughly May 2027, and it is a spending window, not a crisis window - which makes it easy to underestimate.

The cash burn accelerates by design. Capital spending went from $4.4 million in the September 2025 quarter to $23.2 million in March 2026 to $94.8 million in June 2026. Full-year guidance of $350-500 million against roughly $118 million spent in the first half means the second half runs materially harder, so the September and December quarters will print the first genuinely large outflows this company has ever reported. Free cash flow was negative $222 million over the trailing twelve months and gets worse from here, not better.

The funding response is the danger. The $1 billion at-the-market equity facility is open and was drawn on for $54 million in the June quarter. Shares outstanding are already up about 17% in five quarters. Every dollar raised at a lower price buys less and dilutes more, and the share price has fallen from $464.25 to $175.78 over the last year - so the facility is now roughly two and a half times more dilutive per dollar than when it was announced.

The nearest hard date is the September-quarter result in early November 2026. The September quarter has historically been this company's weak delivery quarter: in September 2025 it printed a gross loss of $4.3 million and an operating loss of $16.6 million. A repeat against a cost base that now includes hundreds of new employees in Ohio and Tennessee, a Fluor engineering contract and a Palantir platform would be considerably uglier. Management's own repeated caution that "annual results are more indicative" will not protect the share price on the day.

Two macro pressures compound it. The prevailing market read notes long-dated government bond yields at a nineteen-year high, and a company whose first new cash flows arrive in 2029 is the maximum-duration equity - it takes the full force of a rising discount rate with no near-term earnings to offset it. And the same read notes that the tape has now twice re-priced companies on funding quality, buying those whose cash flow covers their capital spending and selling those it does not. Centrus is the purest example of the punished profile: negative free cash flow, a capital programme twenty times last year's, and equity issuance filling the gap.

Finally, February 2027 brings the 2027 guidance package, which is the first moment management must publicly address the post-waiver revenue bridge. That is a scheduled disclosure risk with no offsetting positive.
positioning_washout:
The shareholder base is a source of risk here, not support - and importantly, the risk is a momentum unwind rather than a mechanical income-mandate exit, because there is no dividend to cut and no yield-focused holder to force out.

The register is thematic and weakly held. The screener puts smart-money ownership at 33 out of 100 against institutional flow of 60 out of 100 - money that arrived on the story rather than on the numbers. The demonstration was on 28 August 2026, when the shares fell 9.8% in a single session with no company news while every uranium and nuclear name fell together: Uranium Energy 9.0%, Denison 7.6%, Energy Fuels 6.8%, Cameco 5.9%, the sector exchange-traded fund 5.8%, Oklo 5.6%, NuScale 4.6%. When one holder sells the theme, they sell all of it, and Centrus - with no earnings cushion - takes the largest hit in the group.

Index membership adds passive holders who will not defend the price. Centrus joined the S&P SmallCap 600 effective 14 July 2026. Those trackers neither add on weakness nor sell on valuation; they simply hold, which removes a slice of the float from the price-discovery process without adding any support. The prevailing market read is explicit that mechanical index effects have stopped paying, so this should not be counted as a positive.

There is a mechanical seller most investors overlook. Roughly $1.18 billion of convertible notes are outstanding, issued in two tranches. Convertible arbitrage desks hold those bonds against a short position in the shares, and as the share price falls their hedge ratio changes in a way that generally requires more shorting, not less. That is real, non-discretionary supply that grows as the stock weakens.

And the usual circuit-breaker has been disabled. The Section 382 rights agreement - a poison-pill structure nominally protecting the company's tax losses - was extended for a seventh time on 18 June 2026 with shareholder approval. Whatever its tax merit, it prevents anyone from building a stake large enough to force a change of course. There will be no activist putting a floor under this, and no strategic buyer accumulating quietly. Management alone decides how long shareholders fund the build.

Insiders have already positioned: zero open-market purchases against eight sales totalling 128,839 shares, during the most favourable news flow the company has ever had.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now, and the reason is arithmetic rather than pessimism about the company.

We think Centrus probably builds the plant. The operational evidence is the strongest part of this file: two years of continuous enrichment, more than 3.9 million machine hours, over 1.6 metric tons of high-assay fuel delivered ahead of schedule, the only American licence for enrichment up to 19.75%, a customer that responded to that performance by signing a contract worth over $1 billion, a first genuinely commercial offtake agreement with X-energy in August 2026, and Fluor running the construction. This is a real franchise being built by people who have so far done what they said.

The problem is what it costs to own that today. At $175.78 the fully diluted equity is $3.85 billion. Against it sits a business that produced $7.4 million of operating profit on $473.9 million of revenue over the last twelve months and burned $222 million of cash. The reported profit of $48.5 million that many investors anchor on is mostly interest earned on money shareholders and bondholders provided. Our sum-of-the-parts - crediting the brokerage book at $300 million, the government services segment at $280 million, the future enrichment plant at $1.40 billion discounted from 2032, and the full $691 million of net cash - reaches about $118 per share. The stock trades roughly half again above that. The favourable case gets to $280, but it needs the 2029 start-up, a construction bill near management's own European benchmark, and enrichment prices holding near $200 per unit. The adverse case reaches $46 and requires only a two-year slip, a cost overrun and mean-reverting prices - not a failure.

Three things tip the judgement. First, roughly three-quarters of today's revenue comes from reselling foreign-sourced enriched uranium under import waivers that cover 2026 and 2027 only, with the new plant not producing until 2029. Nobody has bridged 2028 - not management, and not a single analyst across five earnings calls. Second, the two numbers that determine whether this project creates value - the price per separative work unit realised and the cost to produce one - have been requested directly by analysts and refused on five consecutive calls. We are being asked to underwrite a $3 billion industrial project on faith in the operator, and while the operator has earned some of that faith, the price already assumes all of it. Third, this is not an independent bet. On 28 August 2026 the shares fell 9.8% with no company news while the entire uranium and nuclear complex fell 2% to 9%. The current market read prizes exactly the opposite - positions whose outcome does not hinge on one shared driver - and has twice re-priced companies on funding quality, rewarding those whose cash flow covers their capital spending and selling those it does not. Centrus is the purest example of the profile being sold: a capital programme twenty times last year's, negative cash flow, and an open equity facility filling the gap into a falling price.

On timing: the events that could have re-rated this have already happened and the market has absorbed them. The nearest fixed dates - the September-quarter result in early November 2026 and the 2027 guidance package in February - both skew negative. The one item that could genuinely change our mind before then is the completion of the first commercially manufactured centrifuge at Oak Ridge by year-end, together with a published total project cost. If management put a construction budget and a realised enrichment price on the record and the numbers worked, this would become a different discussion quickly.

We are not down-rating this because the catalyst is spent - a fired event on a clean franchise is neither a mark for nor against in this book. We are down-rating it because the price sits materially above what we can justify for the parts, because the current earnings base is close to zero and legislated to shrink before the new one starts, and because there is no floor: the $31.60 per share of net cash is committed to the build, there is no dividend or buyback, and the Section 382 rights agreement blocks anyone from accumulating a stake large enough to force a change. A pile of cash shareholders cannot reach is not protection.

What we would wait for: a price near our base-case fair value of about $118, or - better - a published project budget and realised enrichment price that let us test the return on the plant directly. Either would move this from a pass to a live discussion.

Over five calls, Centrus has told one story with steadily rising stakes, and the story has changed character completely — from "we are a well-capitalized company waiting for the government to pick us" to "we are a construction company spending several billion dollars."

**Spring 2025 — the applicant.** The first two calls are a lobbying pitch. Management's four "readiness initiatives" (strengthen the balance sheet, restart centrifuge manufacturing, keep the demonstration cascade running, work the politicians) are all framed as evidence for a decision someone else will make. The word that recurs is *awaiting*: "We are awaiting the DOE's decision on how they plan to allocate these funds" (Q1 2025). Management even reads out the letters written on its behalf by Ohio's governor and congressional delegation. The financial story is simple and, at the time, genuinely good: a small brokerage business throwing off cash, $653 million in the bank, and an option on a $3.4 billion federal pot.

**Autumn 2025 — the pivot to capital.** Q3 2025 is the hinge. A new chief financial officer arrives (Todd Tinelli replacing Kevin Harrill), the cash balance jumps past $1.6 billion on an upsized convertible-note deal, and on the same morning the company announces a $1 billion at-the-market equity program — a facility that lets it sell new shares into the open market whenever it chooses. Note the sequencing: the capital came *before* the award. Management's language flips from "awaiting" to "we are seeing growing momentum," and the first outside partner (KHNP/POSCO, a memorandum of understanding, not a contract) is introduced.

**Winter 2025/26 — the build-out is declared.** The Q4 call is the transformation. Centrus announces it will begin commercial centrifuge manufacturing, discloses that the Department of Energy has selected it for a $900 million high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU — fuel enriched to just under 20%, needed by next-generation reactors) award, names Fluor as its engineering and construction partner, and — for the first time in the company's recent history — gives formal annual guidance: revenue of $425–475 million and capital spending of $350–500 million. The critical sentence for anyone underwriting this stock is buried in the prepared remarks: **"Our first new cascade of centrifuges is expected to come online in 2029."**

The company still will not disclose an SWU price, a cost per SWU, a total project cost, or a contract margin. **Score: Medium-High on operations, Low on economics.**

Centrus gave no financial guidance at all until February 2026, which makes the historical track record thin. What exists is good:

- **2026 revenue guidance $425–475 million (Feb 2026) → raised to $450–500 million (May 2026).** Raised within one quarter, and the first half delivered $252.8 million — on track.
- **Piketon hiring "over 50 net new employees" → raised to "over 100."** Delivered ahead of plan.

This is the single strongest credibility marker in the file — a demanding customer with full visibility chose to buy more.
- **Earnings beats.** The screener records beats in 5 of the last 7 quarters (71%), consistent with a management team that guides conservatively where it guides at all.

The offsetting concern is what guidance *omits*. There is no earnings guidance, no free-cash-flow guidance, no total project cost, and no date by which the company will be self-funding. The 2029 first-cascade date is the only forward commitment that really matters to the valuation, and it sits three years beyond any number management is prepared to stand behind. Guidance that covers only the spending side of a multi-billion-dollar build is not a full accountability framework — it is the half of the story management can be confident of hitting.

A smaller flag on sandbagging: revenue guidance was raised on a first half that was, in management's own repeated framing, driven by "delivery timing" the company does not control. Raising an annual number on a timing-driven half is a mild stretch.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions have been asked in nearly identical form across multiple calls and have never been answered.

1. **"What SWU price do you need?"** (Vikram Bagri, Citi, Q3'25). The answer: "I will not be able to name that because that will point to our cost structure." Analysts are asking whether the project clears its hurdle rate. Management is declining to say. This is the single most important unanswered question in the file — the entire investment case is a bet on a spread nobody outside the company can see.

The chief financial officer explicitly did not answer, then pivoted to a European competitor's $2 billion cost for 2.5 million SWU of capacity — a number that, applied to Centrus's planned 3.5 million SWU, implies roughly $2.8 billion of construction spend against $1.87 billion of cash. 3. **"How much of the LEU capacity is captive to HALEU?"** (Lawson Winder, Bank of America, Q4'25). Answered in generalities: "it is our intention... to optimize." The commercial mix that determines revenue per SWU remains undisclosed.

That is a fair point for 2029 but a weakening one for the 2030s, which is exactly the period in which the plant is supposed to earn its return.

**What analysts are not asking, and should be:** what happens in 2028, when the Russian import waivers have expired and the new cascades have not yet started. Not one analyst on these five calls asked management to bridge that gap.

- 🟢 **Operational delivery is genuine and independently verified.** Two years of continuous enrichment, 3.9 million machine hours, deliveries completed ahead of schedule, and a customer (the Department of Energy) that responded by extending and then expanding the contract to over $1 billion (July 2026).

- **"Contingent" is doing enormous work.** The company describes "$2.4 billion in contingent LEU enrichment sales that are all under definitive agreement" (Q1'26). Headline backlog of $4.5 billion is therefore not comparable to a normal industrial backlog.
- **A vocabulary shift from "demonstration" to "commercial."** In 2025 the Piketon cascade was a "demo program" — the chief executive even called it "a bit awkward because the material... is actually useful." - **The new chief financial officer's opening words were about capital, not operations.** Tinelli's first remarks (Q3'25) were "appropriately position our balance sheet and potential partnership network to sufficiently capitalize the company." - **A shift from "we don't provide guidance" to guidance, with the omissions intact.** Harrill in Q1'25: "we don't provide financial guidance." ---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

This is not a company improving; it is a company becoming a different company. Centrus is converting itself from a low-capital brokerage that buys enriched uranium abroad and resells it to US utilities — a business with no moat, thin and erratic margins, and a statutory expiry date — into a capital-intensive industrial enricher whose first new cascade is scheduled for 2029. Management has executed the early stages of that pivot well and has earned genuine credibility on delivery. What it has not done is give investors any way to judge whether the pivot creates value.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing a position:** *the entire investment case is a 2029-and-beyond asset, and the company will not disclose the two numbers that determine whether it is worth building.* Neither the price per separative work unit that Centrus realises nor its cost to produce one has ever been stated. Without that spread, the plant's return on roughly $3 billion of construction spend is unknowable from the outside — investors are underwriting an industrial project on faith in the operator. Between now and then the company earns almost nothing operationally, burns cash, has a $1 billion equity facility open, and watches its main revenue source expire on a legislated schedule. Any position must be sized as venture capital in a listed wrapper, not as a value holding, however far the shares have already fallen from their highs.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and widening.** The moat type is a regulatory licence — Centrus holds the only US authorisation to enrich to 19.75%, and greenfield licensing takes years. That is a real barrier and it is being reinforced: a signed government contract worth over $1 billion, a definitive commercial offtake agreement with X-energy, and physical capacity under construction all deepen the position. But it must be called narrow, not wide, for two reasons the financials make plain. First, the moat protects a business that does not yet generate profit — trailing operating margin is 1.6% and returns on capital, stripped of interest income, are close to zero. Second, gross margin is going the wrong way (26.2% for 2025 and contracting; 28.3% in the latest quarter against 34.9% a year before), because today's revenue comes from the unmoated brokerage, not from the licensed asset. Urenco's US affiliate, Orano and Global Laser Enrichment are all moving, and the licence advantage is a lead measured in years, not a permanent exclusion.

**Secular threat: manageable.** No structural force is eroding the terminal value of uranium enrichment — the opposite is true, since electrification, reactor restarts and the removal of Russian supply all expand the addressable market, and management's cited 24% compound annual growth in the enrichment price curve from 2019 to 2025 is corroborated by the wider market's behaviour. The genuine long-run risk is competitive rather than secular: by the time Centrus's capacity is running at scale in the 2030s, Urenco, Orano and others may have added enough supply to compress the price that makes the project work. That is a cyclical-competitive risk, not a melting base.

**Is the current price a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither, and this is the uncomfortable conclusion. The shares have fallen roughly 62% from their 52-week high, which superficially looks like a fear-print on a quality asset. But even after that fall the business is capitalised at about $3.8 billion on a fully diluted basis against $7.4 million of trailing operating profit and negative $222 million of free cash flow. The decline has removed froth, not created a discount. The cheapness is optical only, because there is almost no current earnings base for the multiple to be cheap against — the price is a claim on 2029.

bull_thesis:
The bullish case is that Centrus Energy is the only company in the United States licensed and physically able to enrich uranium with American technology, that Washington has now put more than a billion dollars behind it in a signed contract, and that the shares have already fallen about 62% from their 52-week high of $464.25 to $175.78 (New York close, 28 August 2026) while the underlying position got stronger rather than weaker.

Crucially, it delivered ahead of schedule: the July 2026 announcement confirms an additional 900 kilograms completed early. The customer with the deepest possible visibility into this operation responded by extending the contract, then signing a definitive one worth over $1 billion including options on 1 July 2026. That is the single hardest piece of third-party validation available.

As the chief executive put it in the first-quarter 2025 call, Centrus holds the only licence permitting enrichment up to 19.75%, and building a competing plant from scratch "takes years and tens of millions of dollars" just to get permitted. Urenco's American affiliate is not licensed for this material; Orano and the laser-enrichment venture are at the announcement stage. For the rest of the decade the competitive set in domestic high-assay fuel is one company.

Demand is not speculative either. Russia's exit from the Western market removes roughly 6.5 million separative work units (the industry's unit of enrichment) of near-term American demand that has to be sourced somewhere else, and management notes the enrichment price curve compounded at about 24% a year from 2019 to 2025. Commercial commitments are converting from talk into contracts: the August 2026 agreement with X-energy is a definitive supply contract that potentially includes customer prepayments, a genuine step up from the 2025 memorandum with the Korean utility KHNP and POSCO. Contracted backlog has grown from $2.3 billion at the end of 2025 to about $4.5 billion, with the contingent enrichment slice alone reaching $3.0 billion.

Execution risk is being deliberately bought down. Fluor - one of the world's larger engineering and construction firms - is the primary contractor at Piketon. Geiger Brothers, who built the existing cascade, handles the ground work. Palantir's data platform is being used to run the supply chain, and management has claimed roughly $300 million of identified cost reductions since January 2026. Hiring is running ahead of plan in both Ohio and Tennessee, and 2026 revenue guidance was raised in May to $450-500 million from $425-475 million.

The balance sheet buys the time this needs. At 30 June 2026 the company held $1.87 billion of cash against $1.18 billion of convertible debt - net cash of $691 million, or about $31.60 for each of the 21.9 million fully diluted shares. If all four hold, a business running 3.5 million separative work units a year at mature cost is worth several billion dollars, and today's price will look like an entry point.

That business has no moat, erratic margins, and a legislated end date. Management disclosed in the third-quarter 2025 call that waivers cover committed deliveries in 2026 and 2027 only. The first new cascade is scheduled for 2029. Across five consecutive earnings calls, not one analyst asked how the company bridges 2028, and management never volunteered it. The most likely shape of the next two years is therefore a shrinking revenue base, an accelerating cash burn, and continued equity issuance.

The economics of the build are undisclosed and unverifiable. Analysts have asked directly and repeatedly for the price per separative work unit Centrus realises and its cost to produce one. The chief executive refused in the third-quarter 2025 call: naming it "will point to our cost structure." The chief financial officer, asked in the second-quarter 2025 call how far the cash would stretch, did not answer, and instead volunteered a European competitor's cost of about $2 billion for 2.5 million separative work units - which implies roughly $2.8 billion for Centrus's planned 3.5 million, against $1.87 billion of cash. That is the only cost anchor on the record, it came from management, and it points to a funding gap. The claimed "$300 million in potential cost savings" cannot be checked because no project budget has ever been published; a saving measured against an undisclosed number is unfalsifiable.

The presentation is drifting promotional. In the June 2026 quarter reported net income of $16.8 million was accompanied by an adjusted figure of $38.7 million - a $22 million gap, the widest yet - while stock-based compensation of $18.1 million in that single quarter exceeded reported profit. Gross margin fell to 28.3% from 34.9% a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share fell 52% year on year. Headline backlog of $4.5 billion is not comparable to an ordinary industrial backlog: management itself labels the $3.0 billion enrichment slice "contingent," meaning contingent on capacity that does not exist, and only about $700 million is deliverable from today's business.

Insiders are voting the other way. Over the most bullish stretch in the company's history there were zero open-market purchases against eight sales totalling 128,839 shares. And the takeover-and-activist route that normally disciplines a company spending shareholders' money for five years before returning any is blocked: the Section 382 rights agreement, a poison-pill mechanism, was extended for a seventh time on 18 June 2026.

Finally, this is not an independent bet. On 28 August 2026 the shares fell 9.8% in one session while Cameco fell 5.9%, Uranium Energy 9.0%, Denison 7.6%, Energy Fuels 6.8%, Oklo 5.6%, NuScale 4.6% and the uranium exchange-traded fund 5.8%. Nothing company-specific happened. The entire position is a levered claim on one shared driver - the market's appetite for the nuclear and artificial-intelligence power build-out - and with no current earnings to cushion it, that claim reprices violently. The 52-week range of $142.13 to $464.25 is the honest picture of how this security behaves.

What would confirm the bear case: a September-quarter result in early November showing another weak delivery quarter against a now much larger cost base; any use of the equity facility at a depressed price; a 2027 guidance package in February that fails to bridge the post-waiver revenue gap; or the first published total project cost coming in above $3 billion.
consensus_delta:

forcing_function:

valley_of_death:
The risky window runs from now through roughly May 2027, and it is a spending window, not a crisis window - which makes it easy to underestimate.

positioning_washout:

The register is thematic and weakly held. The screener puts smart-money ownership at 33 out of 100 against institutional flow of 60 out of 100 - money that arrived on the story rather than on the numbers. The prevailing market read is explicit that mechanical index effects have stopped paying, so this should not be counted as a positive.

There is a mechanical seller most investors overlook. Roughly $1.18 billion of convertible notes are outstanding, issued in two tranches. Convertible arbitrage desks hold those bonds against a short position in the shares, and as the share price falls their hedge ratio changes in a way that generally requires more shorting, not less. That is real, non-discretionary supply that grows as the stock weakens.

And the usual circuit-breaker has been disabled. The Section 382 rights agreement - a poison-pill structure nominally protecting the company's tax losses - was extended for a seventh time on 18 June 2026 with shareholder approval. Whatever its tax merit, it prevents anyone from building a stake large enough to force a change of course. moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now, and the reason is arithmetic rather than pessimism about the company.

We think Centrus probably builds the plant. The operational evidence is the strongest part of this file: two years of continuous enrichment, more than 3.9 million machine hours, over 1.6 metric tons of high-assay fuel delivered ahead of schedule, the only American licence for enrichment up to 19.75%, a customer that responded to that performance by signing a contract worth over $1 billion, a first genuinely commercial offtake agreement with X-energy in August 2026, and Fluor running the construction. The problem is what it costs to own that today. At $175.78 the fully diluted equity is $3.85 billion. Against it sits a business that produced $7.4 million of operating profit on $473.9 million of revenue over the last twelve months and burned $222 million of cash. The reported profit of $48.5 million that many investors anchor on is mostly interest earned on money shareholders and bondholders provided. Our sum-of-the-parts - crediting the brokerage book at $300 million, the government services segment at $280 million, the future enrichment plant at $1.40 billion discounted from 2032, and the full $691 million of net cash - reaches about $118 per share. The stock trades roughly half again above that. The favourable case gets to $280, but it needs the 2029 start-up, a construction bill near management's own European benchmark, and enrichment prices holding near $200 per unit. The adverse case reaches $46 and requires only a two-year slip, a cost overrun and mean-reverting prices - not a failure.

Three things tip the judgement. First, roughly three-quarters of today's revenue comes from reselling foreign-sourced enriched uranium under import waivers that cover 2026 and 2027 only, with the new plant not producing until 2029. Nobody has bridged 2028 - not management, and not a single analyst across five earnings calls. Second, the two numbers that determine whether this project creates value - the price per separative work unit realised and the cost to produce one - have been requested directly by analysts and refused on five consecutive calls. We are being asked to underwrite a $3 billion industrial project on faith in the operator, and while the operator has earned some of that faith, the price already assumes all of it. Third, this is not an independent bet. On 28 August 2026 the shares fell 9.8% with no company news while the entire uranium and nuclear complex fell 2% to 9%. The current market read prizes exactly the opposite - positions whose outcome does not hinge on one shared driver - and has twice re-priced companies on funding quality, rewarding those whose cash flow covers their capital spending and selling those it does not. Centrus is the purest example of the profile being sold: a capital programme twenty times last year's, negative cash flow, and an open equity facility filling the gap into a falling price.

On timing: the events that could have re-rated this have already happened and the market has absorbed them. The nearest fixed dates - the September-quarter result in early November 2026 and the 2027 guidance package in February - both skew negative. The one item that could genuinely change our mind before then is the completion of the first commercially manufactured centrifuge at Oak Ridge by year-end, together with a published total project cost. If management put a construction budget and a realised enrichment price on the record and the numbers worked, this would become a different discussion quickly.

We are not down-rating this because the catalyst is spent - a fired event on a clean franchise is neither a mark for nor against in this book. We are down-rating it because the price sits materially above what we can justify for the parts, because the current earnings base is close to zero and legislated to shrink before the new one starts, and because there is no floor: the $31.60 per share of net cash is committed to the build, there is no dividend or buyback, and the Section 382 rights agreement blocks anyone from accumulating a stake large enough to force a change. A pile of cash shareholders cannot reach is not protection.

What we would wait for: a price near our base-case fair value of about $118, or - better - a published project budget and realised enrichment price that let us test the return on the plant directly. Either would move this from a pass to a live discussion.

interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Centrus Energy Corp. (NYSE: LEU)

**Prepared:** 2026-08-31 · **Price used:** $175.78 (US dollars, NYSE close of Friday 2026-08-28) · **Transcripts reviewed:** Q1 2025 (2025-05-08), Q2 2025 (2025-08-06), Q3 2025 (2025-11-06), Q4/FY 2025 (2026-02-11), Q1 2026 (2026-05-06)

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Over five calls, Centrus has told one story with steadily rising stakes, and the story has changed character completely — from "we are a well-capitalized company waiting for the government to pick us" to "we are a construction company spending several billion dollars."

**Spring 2025 — the applicant.** The first two calls are a lobbying pitch. Management's four "readiness initiatives" (strengthen the balance sheet, restart centrifuge manufacturing, keep the demonstration cascade running, work the politicians) are all framed as evidence for a decision someone else will make. The word that recurs is *awaiting*: "We are awaiting the DOE's decision on how they plan to allocate these funds" (Q1 2025). Management even reads out the letters written on its behalf by Ohio's governor and congressional delegation. The financial story is simple and, at the time, genuinely good: a small brokerage business throwing off cash, $653 million in the bank, and an option on a $3.4 billion federal pot.

**Autumn 2025 — the pivot to capital.** Q3 2025 is the hinge. A new chief financial officer arrives (Todd Tinelli replacing Kevin Harrill), the cash balance jumps past $1.6 billion on an upsized convertible-note deal, and on the same morning the company announces a $1 billion at-the-market equity program — a facility that lets it sell new shares into the open market whenever it chooses. Note the sequencing: the capital came *before* the award. Management's language flips from "awaiting" to "we are seeing growing momentum," and the first outside partner (KHNP/POSCO, a memorandum of understanding, not a contract) is introduced.

**Winter 2025/26 — the build-out is declared.** The Q4 call is the transformation. Centrus announces it will begin commercial centrifuge manufacturing, discloses that the Department of Energy has selected it for a $900 million high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU — fuel enriched to just under 20%, needed by next-generation reactors) award, names Fluor as its engineering and construction partner, and — for the first time in the company's recent history — gives formal annual guidance: revenue of $425–475 million and capital spending of $350–500 million. The critical sentence for anyone underwriting this stock is buried in the prepared remarks: **"Our first new cascade of centrifuges is expected to come online in 2029."**

**Spring 2026 — execution theatre.** Q1 2026 adds a $560 million investment in the Oak Ridge manufacturing plant, three named partners (Fluor, Palantir, Geiger Brothers), a claimed "$300 million in potential cost savings," an exploratory joint venture with Oklo, backlog of $3.9 billion, and two guidance raises (revenue to $450–500 million; Piketon hiring doubled). Momentum is real. But the growth drivers that dominated the 2025 calls — the brokerage business, the delivery-timing mechanics, the Russian supply waivers — have quietly receded from the prepared remarks even though they still generate essentially all of the revenue.

**What was dropped and never replaced.** The 2025 calls repeatedly stressed the company's dependence on shipments from TENEX, the Russian supplier, and the waivers permitting those imports. By Q1 2026 that subject appears only as a reassurance ("waivers... for all currently committed deliveries to U.S. customers in 2026 and 2027") and then vanishes. Those waivers expire. The business that produces roughly three-quarters of today's revenue has a legislated end date, and management has never once explained on these calls what replaces it in 2028 — the gap year between the brokerage running off and the new plant starting up.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "We achieved robust financial results" (repeated every call) | Q1'25 → Q1'26 | Trailing-twelve-month revenue of $474 million produced **operating income of $7.4 million** — an operating margin of 1.6%. Reported net income of $48.5 million over the same period is mostly *interest earned on the cash pile*, not the business. | **Diverges sharply.** The adjective is unsupported. |
| Growth: "revenue... an increase of 30% versus the same quarter last year" | Q3'25 | True for that quarter, but the full-year picture is flat: 2024 revenue $442 million → 2025 $448.7 million, up 1.5%. Quarterly figures swing between $73 million and $176 million purely on delivery timing — management says so itself. | **Technically true, selectively framed.** |
| Margin discipline: "gross margin improved to 35%... reflecting our focus on operational efficiency" | Q2'25 | The very next quarter (Q3'25) printed a **gross loss of $4.3 million**. The latest quarter (Q2'26) shows 28.3% gross margin against 34.9% a year earlier — the direction is down, not up. Full-year 2025 gross margin was 26.2% and contracting. | **Diverges.** Margin is a function of which contracts happen to ship, not of efficiency. Management effectively concedes this elsewhere ("we use average costing"). |
| Earnings quality: "adjusted net income of $38.7 million" | Q2 2026 release | Reported (GAAP) net income for the same quarter was **$16.8 million**, down 42% year over year, with diluted earnings per share of $0.77 against $1.59 — a 52% decline. The $22 million gap between the two figures is the largest the company has presented. Stock-based compensation alone was $18.1 million in the quarter, more than reported net income. | **Story materially richer than the numbers.** |

But it was **bought, not earned**: over the last four quarters the company raised roughly $1.22 billion externally ($782 million of convertible notes in Q3'25, $384 million of equity in Q4'25, $54 million of at-the-market stock sales in Q2'26) while free cash flow ran to **negative $222 million**. A saving measured against an undisclosed number cannot be checked, now or later. Meanwhile capital spending accelerated from $4.4 million (Q3'25) to $94.8 million (Q2'26) per quarter. | **Unfalsifiable claim.** Treat as marketing until a total project cost is published. |

Only about $700 million is brokerage backlog deliverable from today's business. | **Directionally true; the quality of the backlog is far softer than the headline.** |

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising — and increasingly promotional.**

- **Q1 2025 (defensive-hopeful):** "We are awaiting the DOE's decision." Management repeatedly declines to speculate: "I will not venture into predicting what how and when the NNSA may do what. I'll be very careful not to comment on it."
- **Q2 2025 (assertive):** "On the road to energy dominance, nuclear energy is being unleashed." Note the shift into national-mission rhetoric, which from here on substitutes for financial specificity.
- **Q3 2025 (confident, capital-raising):** "Given the market signal and our progress, we believe now it is an appropriate time to raise these funds." The chief executive volunteers that SWU pricing — the price of separative work units, the unit in which enrichment is sold — "is not bad," while refusing to quantify it.
- **Q4 2025 (triumphal):** "2025 was a milestone year." First formal guidance ever. "Operational excellence is nonnegotiable."
- **Q1 2026 (superlative):** "a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reclaim American leadership"; "This was a very successful quarter for the company across all fronts."

The language moved decisively from defensive to offensive across the five calls, which is what you would expect from a company that won its argument. What is worth noting is the *inverse* relationship between rhetorical confidence and financial disclosure: as the tone rose, the specificity around unit economics did not follow. The company still will not disclose an SWU price, a cost per SWU, a total project cost, or a contract margin. The one place specificity increased — annual guidance introduced in Q4 2025 — covers revenue and capital spending, the two figures management most directly controls, and pointedly excludes earnings and cash flow.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium-High on operations, Low on economics.**

Centrus gave no financial guidance at all until February 2026, which makes the historical track record thin. What exists is good:

- **2026 revenue guidance $425–475 million (Feb 2026) → raised to $450–500 million (May 2026).** Raised within one quarter, and the first half delivered $252.8 million — on track.
- **Piketon hiring "over 50 net new employees" → raised to "over 100."** Delivered ahead of plan.
- **HALEU deliveries.** The 900-kilogram Phase 2 milestone was met, and the July 2026 release confirms an additional 900 kilograms completed *ahead of schedule*. The Department of Energy responded by exercising an extension and then signing a contract worth over $1 billion. This is the single strongest credibility marker in the file — a demanding customer with full visibility chose to buy more.
- **Earnings beats.** The screener records beats in 5 of the last 7 quarters (71%), consistent with a management team that guides conservatively where it guides at all.

The offsetting concern is what guidance *omits*. There is no earnings guidance, no free-cash-flow guidance, no total project cost, and no date by which the company will be self-funding. The 2029 first-cascade date is the only forward commitment that really matters to the valuation, and it sits three years beyond any number management is prepared to stand behind. Guidance that covers only the spending side of a multi-billion-dollar build is not a full accountability framework — it is the half of the story management can be confident of hitting.

A smaller flag on sandbagging: revenue guidance was raised on a first half that was, in management's own repeated framing, driven by "delivery timing" the company does not control. Raising an annual number on a timing-driven half is a mild stretch.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions have been asked in nearly identical form across multiple calls and have never been answered.

1. **"What SWU price do you need?"** (Vikram Bagri, Citi, Q3'25). The answer: "I will not be able to name that because that will point to our cost structure." Analysts are asking whether the project clears its hurdle rate. Management is declining to say. This is the single most important unanswered question in the file — the entire investment case is a bet on a spread nobody outside the company can see.
2. **"How far does the cash take you?"** (Nicholas Amicucci, Evercore, Q2'25). The chief financial officer explicitly did not answer, then pivoted to a European competitor's $2 billion cost for 2.5 million SWU of capacity — a number that, applied to Centrus's planned 3.5 million SWU, implies roughly $2.8 billion of construction spend against $1.87 billion of cash. The analyst's dry closing line, "close enough for government work," is a polite acknowledgement of a non-answer.
3. **"How much of the LEU capacity is captive to HALEU?"** (Lawson Winder, Bank of America, Q4'25). Answered in generalities: "it is our intention... to optimize." The commercial mix that determines revenue per SWU remains undisclosed.

A fourth topic analysts pushed on early and management deflected — competition (Sameer Joshi, Q1'25) — has since partly materialised: the chief executive named Urenco's Louisiana affiliate, Orano and Global Laser Enrichment as parties making announcements, and dismissed them on licensing lead times. That is a fair point for 2029 but a weakening one for the 2030s, which is exactly the period in which the plant is supposed to earn its return.

**What analysts are not asking, and should be:** what happens in 2028, when the Russian import waivers have expired and the new cascades have not yet started. Not one analyst on these five calls asked management to bridge that gap.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**Red flags**

- 🔴 **Reported profit is mostly interest income.** Trailing-twelve-month operating income is $7.4 million on $474 million of revenue; reported net income is $48.5 million. The difference is chiefly the return on cash raised from investors. (Q1'26 operating income: $0.8 million. Q2'26: $10.4 million.)
- 🔴 **Cash raised, not earned.** Roughly $1.22 billion of external capital over four quarters against negative $222 million of free cash flow (Q3'25 → Q2'26). Basic share count up 17% in five quarters, with a $1 billion at-the-market program still open (announced Q3'25).
- 🔴 **The capital raise preceded the good news.** The $1 billion equity facility was announced on the Q3 2025 call, months before the January 2026 award. Management framed this as prudence; it also means shareholders funded the option before knowing whether it paid.
- 🔴 **Widening gap between reported and adjusted earnings.** Q2 2026: $16.8 million reported versus $38.7 million adjusted. Stock-based compensation of $18.1 million in one quarter exceeded reported net income.
- 🔴 **The revenue base has a legislated expiry.** Import waivers cover 2026 and 2027 only (disclosed Q3'25). The brokerage segment supplies the great majority of current revenue. Nothing in five calls bridges 2028.
- 🔴 **Insider behaviour contradicts the narrative.** Zero open-market purchases against eight sales totalling 128,839 shares, during the most bullish stretch in the company's history.
- 🔴 **Unfalsifiable cost claims.** "$300 million in potential cost savings" (Q1'26) against a project budget that has never been published.
- 🔴 **A takeover-resistant structure.** The Section 382 rights agreement — a poison-pill mechanism nominally protecting tax loss carryforwards — was extended for a seventh time in June 2026. It also blocks the accumulation of a meaningful stake, which forecloses the activist route that normally disciplines a company spending shareholders' money for five years before returning any.

**Green flags**

- 🟢 **Operational delivery is genuine and independently verified.** Two years of continuous enrichment, 3.9 million machine hours, deliveries completed ahead of schedule, and a customer (the Department of Energy) that responded by extending and then expanding the contract to over $1 billion (July 2026).
- 🟢 **The regulatory position is real.** Centrus holds the only US licence permitting enrichment up to 19.75%. As the chief executive put it in Q1 2025, greenfield licensing "takes years and tens of millions of dollars."
- 🟢 **Backlog is converting from soft to hard.** The August 2026 X-energy agreement is a *definitive* contract with prepayments, not a memorandum — a meaningful upgrade on the KHNP/POSCO understanding of a year earlier.
- 🟢 **The chief financial officer transition brought discipline.** Todd Tinelli introduced trailing-twelve-month reporting to blunt the quarterly-timing distortion — an investor-friendly change that makes the business easier, not harder, to judge.
- 🟢 **Blue-chip execution partners.** Fluor as engineering and construction lead, and Geiger Brothers, who built the existing cascade, reduce first-of-a-kind construction risk.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **"Contingent" is doing enormous work.** The company describes "$2.4 billion in contingent LEU enrichment sales that are all under definitive agreement" (Q1'26). Both halves are true and they pull in opposite directions: the agreements are signed, but the obligations are conditional on capacity being built. Headline backlog of $4.5 billion is therefore not comparable to a normal industrial backlog.
- **A vocabulary shift from "demonstration" to "commercial."** In 2025 the Piketon cascade was a "demo program" — the chief executive even called it "a bit awkward because the material... is actually useful." By July 2026 the company intends to "transition the HALEU production cascade to commercial operation." The asset did not change; the accounting and the framing did.
- **The new chief financial officer's opening words were about capital, not operations.** Tinelli's first remarks (Q3'25) were "appropriately position our balance sheet and potential partnership network to sufficiently capitalize the company." A treasurer's mandate was hired for a manufacturing job — a candid signal that funding, not building, is the binding constraint.
- **A shift from "we don't provide guidance" to guidance, with the omissions intact.** Harrill in Q1'25: "we don't provide financial guidance." Tinelli one year later provides revenue and capital-spending guidance — but nothing on profit or cash. The disclosure improved exactly as far as it flattered.
- **The most revealing competitive answer was a deflection about a benchmark.** When pressed on cash runway, the chief financial officer volunteered a European competitor's capacity cost rather than his own. It is the only cost anchor management has ever put on the record, and it points to a construction bill larger than the balance sheet.
- **Management is explicit that its own results are noise.** "We believe our annual results are more indicative of our progress" appears, near-verbatim, in every single call. That is an honest disclosure and it should be taken at face value: no quarter in this file is evidence of anything.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

This is not a company improving; it is a company becoming a different company. Centrus is converting itself from a low-capital brokerage that buys enriched uranium abroad and resells it to US utilities — a business with no moat, thin and erratic margins, and a statutory expiry date — into a capital-intensive industrial enricher whose first new cascade is scheduled for 2029. Management has executed the early stages of that pivot well and has earned genuine credibility on delivery. What it has not done is give investors any way to judge whether the pivot creates value.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing a position:** *the entire investment case is a 2029-and-beyond asset, and the company will not disclose the two numbers that determine whether it is worth building.* Neither the price per separative work unit that Centrus realises nor its cost to produce one has ever been stated. Without that spread, the plant's return on roughly $3 billion of construction spend is unknowable from the outside — investors are underwriting an industrial project on faith in the operator. Between now and then the company earns almost nothing operationally, burns cash, has a $1 billion equity facility open, and watches its main revenue source expire on a legislated schedule. Any position must be sized as venture capital in a listed wrapper, not as a value holding, however far the shares have already fallen from their highs.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and widening.** The moat type is a regulatory licence — Centrus holds the only US authorisation to enrich to 19.75%, and greenfield licensing takes years. That is a real barrier and it is being reinforced: a signed government contract worth over $1 billion, a definitive commercial offtake agreement with X-energy, and physical capacity under construction all deepen the position. But it must be called narrow, not wide, for two reasons the financials make plain. First, the moat protects a business that does not yet generate profit — trailing operating margin is 1.6% and returns on capital, stripped of interest income, are close to zero. Second, gross margin is going the wrong way (26.2% for 2025 and contracting; 28.3% in the latest quarter against 34.9% a year before), because today's revenue comes from the unmoated brokerage, not from the licensed asset. Urenco's US affiliate, Orano and Global Laser Enrichment are all moving, and the licence advantage is a lead measured in years, not a permanent exclusion.

**Secular threat: manageable.** No structural force is eroding the terminal value of uranium enrichment — the opposite is true, since electrification, reactor restarts and the removal of Russian supply all expand the addressable market, and management's cited 24% compound annual growth in the enrichment price curve from 2019 to 2025 is corroborated by the wider market's behaviour. The genuine long-run risk is competitive rather than secular: by the time Centrus's capacity is running at scale in the 2030s, Urenco, Orano and others may have added enough supply to compress the price that makes the project work. That is a cyclical-competitive risk, not a melting base.

**Is the current price a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither, and this is the uncomfortable conclusion. The shares have fallen roughly 62% from their 52-week high, which superficially looks like a fear-print on a quality asset. But even after that fall the business is capitalised at about $3.8 billion on a fully diluted basis against $7.4 million of trailing operating profit and negative $222 million of free cash flow. The decline has removed froth, not created a discount. The cheapness is optical only, because there is almost no current earnings base for the multiple to be cheap against — the price is a claim on 2029.
